topic: Circular debt: why it keeps growing even after every government promises to fix it
why_it_works: In 2025 banks and government signed a 'landmark' Rs1.225 trillion deal to resolve circular debt — and the very next fiscal year it grew by another Rs364 billion anyway, because the deal restructured the existing debt stock without touching the two things that generate new debt every year: DISCO losses and take-or-pay capacity payments to IPPs.
hook_angle: Contradiction hook: 'In 2025, Pakistan signed a landmark deal to finally resolve circular debt. The next fiscal year, it grew anyway.'
sources: Pakistan Banks Association (2025 circular debt resolution deal); Express Tribune/Shafaqna (Rs364bn FY25-26 rise); Profit by Pakistan Today (Rs1.84tn by Feb 2026); IEEFA (capacity payments crisis); EnergyUpdate (18 May 2026, take-and-pay renegotiation); CRSS/ADB/PACRA (mechanism background)

topic: What China actually gets from the 2026 CPEC revamp and Gwadar expansion
why_it_works: Xi and Shehbaz Sharif announced a 'new broad consensus' on CPEC and Gwadar in May 2026 — framed publicly as connectivity and development, but Pakistan owes China roughly $30B of its $124B external debt, and Gwadar sits inside China's wider String-of-Pearls port network, so the real question is what leverage this creates, not just what gets built.

topic: Pakistan is about to privatize its power distribution companies for the first time — what's actually being sold off
why_it_works: The government is selling FESCO, GEPCO, and IESCO first — the DISCOs with the LOWEST losses, not the worst offenders (PESCO/SEPCO) — a contradiction that reveals the deal is shaped by what's commercially sellable under IMF deadline pressure, not by what's most broken.

topic: Why Pakistan closed its entire border with Afghanistan — and what it's costing both countries
why_it_works: After October 2025 airstrikes and Taliban retaliation over TTP sanctuaries, Pakistan shut every crossing with Afghanistan — bilateral trade has since fallen 40-53%, costing Pakistani exporters an estimated $177 million a month, and a Qatar-mediated ceasefire collapsed within weeks, so this is a live case study in how a security dispute over an unrecognized border (the Durand Line) turns into a self-inflicted trade war neither side can easily walk back from.
hook_angle: Contradiction/question hook: two countries that need each other's trade routes have voluntarily shut them down over a border neither fully agrees is even the border.
sources: Kabul Now (Jan 2026, trade drop); Afghanistan International (53% trade fall); RFE/RL and NPR (Feb-Jun 2026 border closure reporting); OHCHR (Mar 2026 UN call for peace)

topic: The NFC Award: why Pakistan's provinces keep fighting over money that's already supposed to be theirs
why_it_works: The 7th NFC Award's formula was written in 2010 — eight years before the FATA-KP merger — and has simply been extended ever since without being rewritten to account for the merged districts' population, so KP is now suing the federal government in the Federal Constitutional Court over ~Rs964bn it says never reached them under a formula built for a map of Pakistan that no longer exists.

why_it_works: Balochistan has produced more of Pakistan's gas than any other province since the 1950s and has the lowest access to it of any province today — a nearly 70-year-old contradiction that sits underneath a resource-rich-but-poorest-province paradox (Sui gas, Reko Diq, Gwadar) and a security cycle that independent analysts, not just advocacy groups, describe as self-reinforcing rather than resolving.
